analogy.p: A line spectrum is like a barcode. Every product has its own pattern of bars, and the scanner reads the pattern instantly and objectively instead of a cashier trying to recognise the product by eye. In the same way each metal ion has its own pattern of lines, and the spectroscope and detector read the pattern accurately and quickly. The brightness of the lines is like the number of identical products you put on the belt: more of the substance gives a stronger signal. The analogy breaks down because a barcode is printed on the product, whereas the lines only appear when the ions are heated in a flame and give out light.
analogy.t: The barcode scanner at the supermarket

bullets: Instrumental methods are used to **identify** which elements or compounds are present and, in many cases, to **measure how much** is present.
They are **machines**: a sample goes in, a physical measurement is made automatically and the result is displayed or printed as data.
This topic is **triple science (Chemistry paper 2) only**; combined science students do not need it.
The one method you must describe in detail is **flame emission spectroscopy**, used to analyse **metal ions in solution**.
Chemical tests (flame tests, precipitation with sodium hydroxide, acid and carbonate) are the **'wet chemistry'** you already know; instrumental methods are the modern alternative to them.
Examiners expect you to compare the two ideas, so always think 'machine versus eye'.
Typical uses: checking drinking water for metal ions, monitoring pollution, testing blood or soil samples, and quality control in factories.
core.p: **Instrumental methods** are analytical techniques that use **machines (instruments)** to detect and identify **elements and compounds**, rather than relying on a person watching for a colour change or a precipitate in a test tube. AQA names **flame emission spectroscopy** as the example you must know in detail. The instrument takes in a tiny sample, measures a physical property such as the light it gives out, and presents the result as a number, graph or pattern that can be compared with reference data. This matters because modern chemistry in forensics, medicine, water testing and food safety often has to work with very small or very dilute samples.

bullets: Colours in a flame test are judged by eye, so the result is **subjective** and depends on the observer.
**Sodium contamination** is very common and its intense yellow-orange colour can hide the colour of other metals in a mixture.
Chemical tests need a **reasonably large sample**; a tiny amount may not give a visible change.
Most chemical tests are **qualitative** (is it there?), not **quantitative** (how much is there?).
Tests can be **slow** when many samples must be checked one after another.
Some ions give similar results (for example several metal hydroxide precipitates look white), which can cause **confusion**.
These weaknesses are exactly what the advantages of instrumental methods answer.
core.h: Why chemical tests are not always good enough
core.p: Traditional chemical tests rely on a person **seeing** a result: a flame colour, a coloured precipitate, a gas that turns limewater cloudy. These tests are cheap and quick for simple school samples, but they have real weaknesses. Colours are **subjective**, so two people may disagree; a **mixture** of ions can hide each other (for example sodium's strong yellow flame masks weaker colours); and a very small or very dilute sample may give no visible result at all. The tests also usually tell you **whether** an ion is present, not **how much**. Instrumental methods were developed to overcome these problems.

bullets: **Accurate**: the machine measures exactly, with results that are **less affected by human error** or opinion.
**Sensitive**: able to detect **tiny amounts** of a substance, even at very low concentration (for example mg per dm³).
**Rapid**: analysis is **fast**, so many samples can be tested in a short time.
Only a **small sample** is needed, which is important if the sample is rare, valuable or limited.
Results are **objective numerical data**, so they can be stored, compared and repeated.
Many instruments give **quantitative** results (concentration), not just a yes/no answer.
Mark scheme phrase: 'instrumental methods are more accurate, more sensitive and faster than chemical tests'.
core.p: The AQA specification gives three headline advantages: instrumental methods are **accurate**, **sensitive** and **rapid**. Learn these three words and be able to explain each one. They are accurate because a detector measures the light or signal electronically and removes human judgement. They are sensitive because they can detect and measure **very small amounts** of a substance in a sample. They are rapid because a result can appear in seconds or minutes and many samples can be run automatically. A further advantage is that only a **small sample** is needed, which is vital when evidence is limited, such as at a crime scene.

bullets: It analyses **metal ions** (for example Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cu²⁺) that are dissolved in a **solution**.
The sample is placed in a **flame**, which supplies the energy needed to make the ions emit light.
The emitted light is passed into a **spectroscope**, which splits it into different wavelengths.
The output is a **line spectrum**, a pattern of lines at particular wavelengths.
The **positions** of the lines identify which metal ions are present.
The **intensity (brightness)** of the lines is used to work out how concentrated each ion is.
It is the instrumental equivalent of the **flame test** (a chemical test).
core.h: Flame emission spectroscopy: what it is used for
core.p: **Flame emission spectroscopy** is an instrumental method used to analyse **metal ions in solutions**. A solution containing the unknown metal ions is introduced into a flame, the metal ions give out light, and an instrument called a **spectroscope** separates that light into its component wavelengths. The output is a **line spectrum**. The specification says this output can be analysed in two ways: to **identify the metal ions** in a solution and to **measure their concentrations**. It is therefore a more powerful, objective version of the flame test you have already met.

bullets: **Step 1:** a **solution** of the sample is prepared (a solid must first be dissolved, often in dilute acid or water).
**Step 2:** the solution is fed into the **flame**, usually as a fine spray or mist.
**Step 3:** the heat of the flame makes the metal ions give out **light of characteristic wavelengths**.
**Step 4:** the light passes through a **spectroscope** (a prism or grating) which separates it into its wavelengths.
**Step 5:** a **detector** measures the position and brightness of each line.
**Step 6:** the output is displayed as a **line spectrum** and analysed by comparing it with **known reference spectra**.
Between samples the instrument is flushed with distilled water so that one sample does not **contaminate** the next.
core.h: Flame emission spectroscopy: the method step by step
core.p: Although you are not asked to build the machine, you must be able to describe the sequence of events in order. The sample solution is first fed into the instrument, usually as a fine spray, and carried into a flame. The heat of the flame excites the metal ions so that they emit light. This light is collected and passed through a **spectroscope**, which spreads it out into a spectrum. A **detector** then records the wavelengths and the intensity of each line, and the instrument (usually connected to a computer) displays the result as a line spectrum or a set of numbers.

bullets: Heat from the flame transfers energy to **electrons** in the metal ions.
Electrons jump to **higher energy levels** (they become 'excited').
Excited electrons fall back down and release the energy as **light**.
A **bigger energy gap** gives light of **shorter wavelength**; a smaller gap gives longer wavelength.
Each element has its own **set of energy gaps**, so its own **fingerprint** of lines.
This is why sodium always gives a strong yellow line at about **589 nm** and lithium a red line at about **671 nm**.
Because only certain gaps exist, the light appears as **separate lines**, not a continuous rainbow.
core.h: Why different ions give different lines (extension)
core.p: This explanation goes slightly beyond what AQA tests, but it helps you remember why the method works. The flame gives the ions energy. The **electrons** in each metal ion absorb some of this energy and move to higher energy levels. These excited electrons are unstable, so they quickly fall back to lower levels. As they fall they give out the extra energy as **light**. The size of each energy gap is **fixed** for a particular element, and the wavelength (colour) of the light depends on the size of the gap, so every metal produces its own **characteristic set of lines**.

bullets: Each metal ion has a **unique pattern** of lines, which acts as its **fingerprint**.
Compare the **wavelength positions** of lines in the unknown with those of the reference spectra.
A metal is present only if **all** of its lines appear in the unknown spectrum.
A **mixture** shows the lines of **each** ion at once, overlaid on the same spectrum.
Lines in the unknown that match **no** reference may mean another ion that is not in the reference data.
Reference points (typical): lithium about **671 nm**, sodium about **589 nm**, potassium about **767 nm**. Exam papers usually give you the values.
In an exam, quote the line positions you matched, for example 'lines at 589 and 767 match sodium and potassium'.
core.h: Reading a line spectrum to identify ions
core.p: A line spectrum is like a **barcode** for a metal. To identify the ions in an unknown sample you compare the **positions of the lines** in its spectrum with the lines in the reference spectra of known metals. If every line from a known metal appears in the unknown spectrum at the same position, that metal is present. If the unknown spectrum contains lines from **two** metals, both are present, because the spectra simply **add together**. The skill examiners test is careful matching: line positions must line up exactly, and a metal is only confirmed if all of its characteristic lines are present.

bullets: **Higher concentration** of the ion means a **more intense** line.
**Calibration** uses several **standard solutions** of known concentration.
Plot **concentration (x-axis)** against **intensity (y-axis)** and draw a **line of best fit**.
Measure the unknown's intensity, then **read across to the line and down** to find the concentration.
If the line goes through the origin, **concentration = intensity ÷ gradient**.
Concentrations are usually given in **mg per dm³** or **mol per dm³**.
If a sample is **too concentrated**, it is **diluted** by a known factor and the answer is multiplied back (see worked example).
core.h: Measuring concentration with a calibration graph
core.p: As well as the **position** of the lines, the **brightness (intensity)** of a line carries information. A solution with more metal ions in it emits more light, so its line is brighter. To turn intensity into concentration, the instrument is first **calibrated**: solutions of **known concentration** of the metal ion are measured and their intensities are plotted on a **calibration graph** (concentration on the x-axis, intensity on the y-axis). The intensity of the unknown sample is then measured and its concentration is read from the graph. Over the working range the graph is usually a straight line, and when it passes through the origin intensity is **directly proportional** to concentration.

bullets: Label axes: 'Concentration of metal ion (mg per dm³)' and 'Intensity (arbitrary units)'.
Use a **ruler** and a straight line of best fit; do not join dot to dot.
Draw **construction lines** to the axes so the examiner can see how you read the value.
**Interpolation** (inside the range of standards) is more reliable than **extrapolation** (outside).
A **gradient** is calculated as change in y ÷ change in x using a large triangle.
Check the answer is sensible: a sample that is brighter than a standard must have a higher concentration than that standard.
If a result must be quoted, give **units** and a sensible number of **significant figures**.
core.h: Graph and data skills for this topic
core.p: Calibration questions are a good source of 'maths in chemistry' marks. Use a sharp pencil and a ruler, choose scales that use more than half of each axis, label both axes **with units**, and plot points accurately. Draw a straight **line of best fit** (it need not go through every point, but it should balance points on either side). Always show the lines you used to read a value, because the examiner awards marks for the method. Reading a value **within** the range of your standards is **interpolation** and is reliable, whereas reading beyond the highest standard is **extrapolation** and is much less reliable.

bullets: **Flame test**: cheap, simple, no training, good for a quick classroom check on a single metal.
**Flame test limits**: subjective colour, masked by sodium, needs more sample, no concentration.
**Flame emission spectroscopy**: objective, accurate, sensitive, rapid and quantitative.
**Spectroscopy limits**: the instrument is **expensive**, needs **training**, regular **calibration** and maintenance.
Spectroscopy needs the sample as a **solution**, so preparation is required.
It detects mainly **metal ions**, so other tests are needed for non-metal ions such as halides or sulfates.
Conclude with a judgement such as 'for a small forensic sample spectroscopy is better because it is more sensitive'.
core.h: Comparing flame emission spectroscopy with chemical tests
core.p: A very common exam question asks you to evaluate the two approaches. A balanced answer gives at least one advantage and one disadvantage and ends with a conclusion matched to the context. For routine classroom work, a chemical flame test is cheap, needs no special equipment and gives a rough answer in seconds. For analysing a tiny, dilute, mixed sample, or when a concentration is needed, flame emission spectroscopy is far superior. Linking your answer to the context (a forensic sample, a river water survey, a school lab) earns the evaluation mark.

bullets: **Calibration errors** (wrong standard concentrations) make every result inaccurate.
**Contamination**, especially sodium from glassware, skin or tap water, creates false lines.
**Overlapping lines** from different ions can make a mixture hard to interpret.
**Dilution errors** are multiplied when the answer is scaled up.
**Equipment cost** and the need for trained operators limit where it can be used.
The sample is **used up** (it is burned in the flame) and must be a **solution**.
Good practice: rinse with **distilled water** between samples and repeat measurements to check **reproducibility**.
core.p: No method is perfect, and examiners like students who can name realistic limitations. Instrument methods depend on correct calibration: if the standards are made up wrongly or are contaminated, every result will be wrong, however modern the machine. In a mixture, lines from different ions can lie **very close together** and overlap, making them hard to separate. Contamination from glassware, from fingers, or from the previous sample, especially with sodium which is everywhere, can add unwanted lines. The method also destroys the sample and cannot be used on solids until they are dissolved.

bullets: Spectroscopy lets scientists identify elements from the **light they emit**, even from very small samples.
Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered **caesium** and **rubidium** using spectroscopy in the 1860s.
**Helium** was first detected in the spectrum of the **Sun** before being found on Earth.
Astronomers still use the same idea to work out which elements are in **stars** from the light they give out.
This shows that new technology can **extend scientific knowledge**, a typical 'How Science Works' idea.
The story is context only; you will not be asked to recall the dates, but it makes a good example in an essay-style answer.
core.h: A historical link: spectroscopy and new elements
core.p: Flame spectroscopy has a famous history that shows how the method is more sensitive than the human eye. In the 1860s the German scientists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff used spectroscopy to study flames and discovered two new elements, **caesium** and **rubidium**, from the unfamiliar lines in their spectra. Later, a bright yellow line seen in the spectrum of light from the Sun in 1868 led scientists to propose a new element that they named **helium** (after the Greek word for the Sun), many years before it was found on Earth. These examples show how a line spectrum can identify elements that chemical tests could not.

bullets: Name the method in full: **flame emission spectroscopy**.
Describe in order: solution → flame → light emitted → spectroscope → line spectrum → compare with known spectra.
State **two links**: line **position** identifies the ion; line **intensity** gives the concentration.
Use the phrase **'accurate, sensitive and rapid'** when asked for advantages.
For data questions, **quote numbers** from the question in your answer.
For evaluation, give **one advantage, one disadvantage and a conclusion** that fits the context.
Link to other topics: **flame tests** (4.8.3), **Group 1 metals** (4.1.2), **concentration calculations** (4.3.5).
core.h: Putting it together: answering exam questions
core.p: Questions on this topic follow a few predictable patterns: name the advantages, describe the method, interpret a line spectrum, use a calibration graph, and evaluate against chemical tests. For a 'describe' question, write the steps in order using the key words flame, spectroscope, line spectrum and compare. For an 'interpret' question, quote evidence from the data. For a calculation, show every step and include units. Keep your language precise: say 'the ions emit light' rather than 'the flame changes colour', and 'line spectrum' rather than 'colours'.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark):** 'flame emission spectroscopy'. Spell it correctly and name the output as a **line spectrum**.
**Advantages (2 marks):** two of 'accurate', 'sensitive', 'rapid'/'fast', 'only a small sample needed', each with a short reason.
**Describe the method (3 to 4 marks):** solution put in flame → ions give out light → light passes through a spectroscope → line spectrum produced → compared with known spectra.
**Identify ions from a spectrum (2 to 3 marks):** state which lines match which metal, quote wavelengths, and state which reference metals do **not** match.
**Calibration graph (3 marks):** plot accurately (1), line of best fit (1), read value using construction lines (1). Units are needed on the answer.
**Concentration calculation:** show gradient or ratio working, then divide; multiply by the dilution factor if the sample was diluted.
**Compare with chemical tests (up to 6 marks):** at least two advantages, one disadvantage, and a conclusion linked to the context to reach the top level.
**Command words:** 'describe' = steps in order; 'explain' = give reasons using 'because'; 'evaluate' = weigh good and bad points and reach a judgement.
**Use key vocabulary:** line spectrum, intensity, wavelength, concentration, calibration, standard solution.
**Check units:** concentration in mg per dm³ or mol per dm³, wavelength in nm.
**Triple only:** this appears on Chemistry paper 2 and counts as 'analysis and application' content, so expect data to be provided.

mistakes.r: Give the three named advantages: more accurate, more sensitive and faster, and explain each, for example 'can detect very small amounts'.
mistakes.w: 'Instrumental methods are better because they are quicker.' (only one reason)

mistakes.r: In flame emission spectroscopy the light is analysed by a spectroscope and detector to produce a line spectrum; it is not judged by eye.
mistakes.w: 'The flame changes colour so you can see the metal.'

mistakes.r: Position (wavelength) identifies the ion; the intensity (brightness) of the line is used to measure concentration.
mistakes.w: 'The position of the line tells you the concentration.'

mistakes.r: It is used to analyse metal ions in solution. Non-metal ions need other tests.
mistakes.w: 'Flame emission spectroscopy identifies any ion, including chloride and sulfate.'

mistakes.r: Draw a straight line that passes close to the points with roughly equal numbers either side (through the origin if the data supports it).
mistakes.w: 'The line of best fit must go through every point.'

mistakes.r: The sample is a solution of the metal ions, introduced into the flame.
mistakes.w: 'The sample is a solid put straight into the machine.'

mistakes.r: If a sample was diluted, multiply the concentration read from the graph by the dilution factor.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply back after diluting a sample.

mistakes.r: A mixture produces the lines of each ion in the same spectrum; match every line to a reference.
mistakes.w: 'Lines from two ions mean one ion is impure.'

mistakes.r: Say why: it is objective, not affected by human judgement, and the results can be repeated and recorded.
mistakes.w: Writing 'It is more reliable' with no explanation.

summary: You must know that instrumental methods (machines) such as flame emission spectroscopy identify elements and compounds, and measure concentrations of metal ions in solution, more accurately, sensitively and rapidly than chemical tests; you need to describe the method, interpret a line spectrum and use a calibration graph (triple only). It matters because modern analysis of water, food, medicines and forensic samples depends on these machines.

terms.d: A way of analysing a sample using a machine that makes a physical measurement automatically, instead of a chemical test judged by eye.
An instrumental method in which a solution of metal ions is put into a flame and the light emitted is analysed with a spectroscope to identify the ions and measure their concentration.
An instrument that splits light into its different wavelengths to produce a spectrum.
The output from flame emission spectroscopy: a pattern of lines at particular wavelengths that is characteristic of each metal ion.
The distance between two matching points on a wave; for visible light it determines the colour. Measured in nanometres (nm).
The brightness of a line in a spectrum; it increases as the concentration of the ion increases.
The amount of a substance dissolved in a given volume of solution, for example in mg per dm³ or mol per dm³.
A graph of the signal (intensity) against concentration for standard solutions of known concentration, used to find the concentration of an unknown sample.
A solution whose concentration is accurately known, used to calibrate an instrument.
Able to detect very small amounts of a substance.
Analysis that tells you which substances are present.
Analysis that tells you how much of a substance is present.
Reading a value from a graph that lies within the range of the plotted data.
Unwanted substances getting into a sample, which can give false results.

worked.ans: 45 mg per dm³ of potassium ions.
worked.q: A flame emission spectrometer is calibrated with standard solutions of potassium ions. The intensities were: 10 mg per dm³ gave 20 units; 20 mg per dm³ gave 40 units; 40 mg per dm³ gave 80 units; 60 mg per dm³ gave 120 units. A water sample gave an intensity of 90 units. Find the concentration of potassium ions. (3 marks)
steps: Look at the pattern: intensity ÷ concentration = 20 ÷ 10 = 2, and 40 ÷ 20 = 2, 80 ÷ 40 = 2, 120 ÷ 60 = 2, so the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 2 units per (mg per dm³).
Concentration = 90 ÷ 2 = 45 mg per dm³ (check: 90 lies between the 80 and 120 standards, so 40 to 60 is the expected range: yes).
Because 90 lies within the range of the standards this is an interpolation, so it is reliable.

worked.q: A student dilutes a salt solution 10 times (1 cm³ of sample made up to 10 cm³) and measures sodium ions by flame emission spectroscopy. Using the same calibration, the diluted sample reads 36 mg per dm³. What was the concentration of sodium ions in the original sample? (2 marks)
steps: The diluted sample reads 36 mg per dm³.
The dilution factor is 10 (10 cm³ ÷ 1 cm³).
Original concentration = measured concentration × dilution factor = 36 × 10 = 360 mg per dm³.

worked.ans: Sodium ions and potassium ions are present, and lithium ions are absent. Advantages: it is more sensitive and more accurate than a flame test, and the sodium flame colour cannot hide the potassium because each ion's lines appear separately in the spectrum.
worked.q: A line spectrum from an unknown solution has lines at 589 nm and 767 nm. Reference lines: lithium 671 nm, sodium 589 nm, potassium 767 nm. Identify the metal ions and give two advantages of using this method rather than a flame test. (4 marks)
steps: Match 589 nm with the sodium reference, so sodium ions are present.
Match 767 nm with the potassium reference, so potassium ions are present.
There is no line at 671 nm, so lithium ions are not present.
Advantages: objective, so not affected by the sodium yellow flame masking potassium's colour; sensitive, so tiny amounts are detected; and it can measure concentration.
